title: Tramadol and Alcohol: Why the Mix Is Dangerous and How Long to Wait
excerpt: Why tramadol and alcohol shouldn't be mixed: slowed breathing, seizures, and serotonin syndrome, plus who to ask before drinking again and the emergency signs to know.
metaDescription: Tramadol and alcohol can slow breathing and raise seizure and serotonin risks. Learn why to avoid it and the emergency signs to know.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** don't drink while you're taking tramadol. Tramadol is an opioid painkiller, and alcohol slows your brain and breathing in the same direction it does. Together they can cause heavy sedation, dangerously slow breathing, and in the worst cases coma or death. Tramadol also has two extra risks that most opioids don't: it can trigger seizures, and it can contribute to serotonin syndrome, a dangerous overload of the brain chemical serotonin. The FDA puts the alcohol and sedative warning in a boxed warning on tramadol's label, which is the strongest warning it uses.

**The quick rules:** Don't drink at all while you're taking tramadol, and ask your prescriber or pharmacist when it's safe to drink again after you stop. Never take tramadol for a hangover. Never take an extra dose because you've been drinking and the pain feels worse. If you already mixed the two, don't drive, don't drink any more, don't take your next dose until you've talked to a pharmacist, and stay with someone who can watch your breathing. If someone is very hard to wake, breathing slowly or noisily, or has blue or gray lips, call 911.

> **This is not medical advice.** This article explains how tramadol and alcohol interact based on the official prescribing information and general research. It is not a substitute for your doctor or pharmacist, who know your dose, your other medicines, and your health history. **Don't drink alcohol while on tramadol**, and don't stop tramadol on your own without talking to your doctor. **Call 911 right away if** someone who took tramadol and alcohol is hard to wake, breathing slowly or shallowly, making gurgling or snoring sounds they can't be woken from, has a seizure, or has blue or gray lips or fingertips. In the US you can also call Poison Control at **1-800-222-1222** for advice at any hour.

## How Tramadol and Alcohol Interact: The Three Risks in Plain Words

Tramadol is sold as Ultram, Ultram ER, ConZip, and many generics. It's also combined with acetaminophen in a product called Ultracet. Doctors often prescribe it for moderate pain after an injury, surgery, or a dental procedure, and sometimes for longer-term pain such as arthritis.

What makes tramadol unusual is that it works in two ways at once:

1. **It acts like an opioid.** Tramadol itself is a weak opioid, but your liver turns part of each dose into a much stronger one, a compound called O-desmethyltramadol (often shortened to M1). This happens through a liver enzyme called CYP2D6. M1 latches onto the same opioid receptors in the brain that morphine and oxycodone do.
2. **It boosts serotonin and norepinephrine.** Tramadol also blocks the brain from reabsorbing these two chemical messengers, a bit like some antidepressants do. That's part of how it eases pain, and it's also where its unusual side effects come from.

Alcohol collides with both of those mechanisms. Here's how.

### Risk 1: Slowed breathing and heavy sedation

This is the biggest danger, and it's the one the boxed warning is about. Opioids slow the part of your brainstem that controls breathing. Alcohol is a depressant that also dampens the brain and slows breathing. The two effects stack on top of each other, so the result can be much stronger than either one alone.

In practice, that can look like:

- Feeling far drunker and sleepier than the amount you drank would explain
- Dizziness, poor coordination, and falls
- Slow, shallow breathing, especially once you fall asleep
- Being very hard to wake up

Sleep is the dangerous part. When you're awake, your brain keeps reminding you to breathe. Once you're asleep after drinking on tramadol, that drive can fade, and nobody may notice. Many opioid-and-alcohol deaths happen when someone "just went to bed."

The FDA's label for tramadol, like other opioid labels, warns that using it with other central nervous system depressants, a group that includes alcohol, benzodiazepines such as Xanax, and sleeping pills, can cause profound sedation, respiratory depression, coma, and death. It tells patients not to drink alcohol while taking it.

### Risk 2: Seizures

Tramadol can cause seizures, even at normal prescribed doses, and the risk rises at higher doses. This is one of the ways it differs from most other opioids. The prescribing information lists several things that raise the seizure risk further, including a history of seizures or epilepsy, head injury, and alcohol or drug withdrawal.

Alcohol pushes on the same weak spot from two directions, which is why this pairing is worse than it first looks:

- **Tramadol lowers the seizure threshold.** The seizure threshold is how much strain it takes before the brain's electrical activity tips into a seizure. Tramadol lowers it, so a smaller push is enough. Drinking adds that push: dehydration, low blood sugar, and broken sleep all strain the brain further.
- **Alcohol withdrawal lowers it too.** As alcohol wears off, the brain rebounds into an overexcited state, and in people who drink heavily or regularly the hours and days after drinking carry a real seizure risk on their own. Taking tramadol during that window stacks two threshold-lowering effects on top of each other. That includes the morning after a big night.

If you have ever had a seizure, or you drink heavily most days, tell your prescriber before you start tramadol. It may not be the right painkiller for you.

### Risk 3: Serotonin syndrome

Because tramadol raises serotonin, it can contribute to serotonin syndrome, a condition where too much serotonin builds up. Symptoms range from mild (shivering, sweating, diarrhea) to life-threatening (high fever, muscle rigidity, seizures).

To be accurate: alcohol isn't a major cause of serotonin syndrome on its own. The real danger comes from tramadol combined with other medicines that also raise serotonin, such as SSRI and SNRI antidepressants (Zoloft, Lexapro, Prozac, Cymbalta, Effexor), MAO inhibitors, triptan migraine drugs, and some others. The alcohol connection is indirect but real: many people who drink socially also take one of these antidepressants, and alcohol makes it harder to notice early symptoms. Agitation, sweating, a racing heart, and shakiness can all be written off as "just a hangover" when something more serious is going on.

If you take an antidepressant, read our guides on [Zoloft and alcohol](/never-hungover/zoloft-and-alcohol) and [antidepressants and alcohol](/never-hungover/antidepressants-and-alcohol), and make sure the doctor prescribing tramadol knows about it.

## Can You Have One Drink on Tramadol?

This is the question most people really want answered, so here it is directly: no. The label tells patients not to drink on tramadol, and there's no amount that's known to be safe.

The reason doctors won't give you a "safe" number is that the effect varies so much from person to person:

- **Your genes matter.** Some people have a version of the CYP2D6 enzyme that works very fast. These "ultra-rapid metabolizers" turn tramadol into its strong opioid form faster and in larger amounts, so they can get much stronger opioid effects from a normal dose. Most people don't know which type they are. The FDA's concern about this is why, since 2017, tramadol has been contraindicated in children under 12, and in children under 18 after tonsil or adenoid surgery.
- **Your dose and timing matter.** Drinking an hour after a dose, when blood levels are near their peak, is not the same as drinking at the end of a course.
- **Other medicines matter.** Sleeping pills, anti-anxiety medicines, muscle relaxers, gabapentin, and sedating antihistamines all add to the sedation.
- **Age, weight, and health matter.** Older adults, smaller people, and people with lung problems such as COPD or sleep apnea, or with kidney or liver problems, are more sensitive.

Because nobody can predict in advance how strongly the two will interact in their body, there's no small amount that counts as safe. The answer is not to drink while you're on tramadol. If you have an event coming up during your course, tell your prescriber so they can help you plan your pain treatment around it.

## How Long After Tramadol Can You Drink?

There's no official waiting period printed on the label, and this is not a number to work out yourself. How long tramadol stays active depends on your dose, whether it's an extended-release form, your genes, your age, and how well your kidneys and liver are working. Older adults and people with kidney or liver problems clear it more slowly.

| Situation | What to do |
|---|---|
| Taking tramadol now (any form) | Don't drink. |
| Extended-release tramadol (Ultram ER, ConZip) | Don't drink. The drug is released over many hours, so it stays active longer than the immediate-release tablet. |
| Tramadol with acetaminophen (Ultracet) | Don't drink. You also have the acetaminophen liver warning to think about. |
| Finished your last dose | Ask your prescriber or pharmacist when it's safe to drink again. They know your dose and health. |

### How long after drinking can you take tramadol?

Don't take tramadol while alcohol may still be in your system, and remember that after a heavy night it can still be in your blood the next morning. If you're in pain and due a dose after drinking, call your pharmacist and ask before you take it.

## Never Take Tramadol for a Hangover

Some people have leftover tramadol from an old prescription and reach for it the morning after a big night. Please don't. It's one of the worst choices you can make for a hangover:

- **Alcohol may still be in your system.** The morning after heavy drinking, your blood alcohol may not be zero yet. Adding an opioid on top of that is exactly the combination the boxed warning is about.
- **Your seizure threshold may already be lower.** The morning after is when alcohol withdrawal starts, and poor sleep, dehydration, and low blood sugar push in the same direction as tramadol.
- **Both can lower blood sugar.** Tramadol's label includes a warning about low blood sugar, and heavy drinking can also lower it, especially if you didn't eat.
- **Nausea gets worse.** Tramadol commonly causes nausea, vomiting, and dizziness. So does a hangover.
- **It's not prescribed for you, now.** Tramadol is a federally controlled substance in the US (Schedule IV since 2014). Taking someone else's, or an old prescription for a new problem, removes the doctor from the decision entirely.

If you have a hangover headache, the better options are water, food, rest, and, if needed, a single label dose of an over-the-counter pain reliever after you've eaten and the alcohol has cleared. Each one has its own alcohol considerations; see our guides on [ibuprofen and alcohol](/never-hungover/ibuprofen-and-alcohol) and [Tylenol and alcohol](/never-hungover/tylenol-and-alcohol).

## "Tramadol Hangover": Why You Might Feel Worse the Next Day

People sometimes search for a "tramadol hangover," meaning they took tramadol, drank, and feel terrible the next day. That rough morning usually comes from several things at once:

- **Lingering sedation.** Tramadol and alcohol both affect sleep quality, and the drug may still be in your system, leaving you groggy and foggy.
- **Nausea and constipation.** Both are common tramadol side effects, and alcohol irritates the gut too.
- **Dehydration and headache** from the alcohol itself.
- **Withdrawal-type symptoms.** If you've been taking tramadol regularly and skipped or delayed a dose, you can feel anxious, sweaty, restless, and achy. Tramadol withdrawal can also cause unusual symptoms such as tingling or feeling detached, because of its effect on serotonin and norepinephrine.

Feeling bad the next day is a signal to stop combining the two, not something to treat with more tramadol. If you've been taking tramadol for more than a couple of weeks and want to stop, ask your doctor how to taper. Stopping suddenly can bring on withdrawal symptoms.

## Tramadol, Alcohol, and the Acetaminophen in Ultracet

If your prescription is Ultracet or a generic "tramadol/APAP" (APAP is an abbreviation for acetaminophen), you're dealing with two separate alcohol warnings at once. The tramadol part carries the breathing, sedation, and seizure risks above. The acetaminophen part carries a liver risk, which is highest for people who have 3 or more drinks a day.

This also creates a hidden-dose problem. If you take Ultracet and then add Tylenol, NyQuil, or another product with acetaminophen, you can go over the daily limit without realizing it. Check the Drug Facts box of anything else you take for "acetaminophen" or "APAP." Our [Tylenol and alcohol guide](/never-hungover/tylenol-and-alcohol) explains the liver side in detail.

## Extended-Release Tramadol and Alcohol

Extended-release tramadol is designed to release the drug slowly over about a day. Two things matter here:

- **It stays in your system longer.** Because each tablet keeps working for many hours, there isn't a "safe gap" during the day where you can fit in a drink.
- **The tablet must stay intact.** Crushing, chewing, splitting, or dissolving an extended-release tablet can release the whole dose at once, which can be fatal. Alcohol can make some extended-release opioid products release their drug faster than intended, which is part of why these labels are so firm about avoiding alcohol.

If you're on an extended-release form, treat the no-alcohol rule as covering your entire course.

## Who Is at Highest Risk

The tramadol and alcohol combination is more dangerous for people who:

- **Also take other sedating medicines**, such as benzodiazepines (Xanax, Valium, Klonopin), sleeping pills (Ambien), gabapentin or pregabalin, muscle relaxers, or sedating antihistamines (Benadryl). See our guides on [Xanax and alcohol](/never-hungover/xanax-and-alcohol) and [gabapentin and alcohol](/never-hungover/gabapentin-and-alcohol).
- **Take antidepressants or migraine medicines** that raise serotonin.
- **Have a history of seizures**, head injury, or heavy daily drinking.
- **Are older adults**, who clear the drug more slowly and are more sensitive to sedation and falls.
- **Have lung or breathing problems**, such as COPD, asthma, or sleep apnea.
- **Have kidney or liver disease**, which slows how fast tramadol is cleared.
- **Are new to tramadol** or just had a dose increase, because your body hasn't adjusted yet.
- **Are combining it with other opioids.** If you've been prescribed something stronger in the past, our [oxycodone and alcohol](/never-hungover/oxycodone-and-alcohol) guide covers the same breathing danger in more depth.

## What to Do If You've Already Mixed Tramadol and Alcohol

If you've already had alcohol on tramadol, even if you feel normal, treat the rest of the night carefully. Breathing problems can start later, once you're asleep:

1. **Stop drinking now**, and drink water instead.
2. **Don't take your next tramadol dose** until you've talked to a pharmacist or doctor. Many pharmacies have a 24-hour line.
3. **Don't take anything else that makes you drowsy**, including sleep aids, Benadryl, or NyQuil.
4. **Don't drive** or operate anything risky.
5. **Don't be alone.** Tell someone what you took and ask them to check on you, especially once you go to sleep.
6. **Sleep on your side**, not on your back, in case you vomit.

If you feel much more drunk or sleepy than usual, call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222 (US) for advice. They're free, confidential, and open around the clock.

## Emergency Signs: When to Call 911

Call 911 right away if someone who has taken tramadol and alcohol:

- Can't be woken up, or keeps falling back asleep mid-sentence
- Is breathing very slowly, shallowly, or has stopped breathing
- Is making deep snoring or gurgling sounds and won't wake up
- Has blue, gray, or pale lips or fingertips, or cold, clammy skin
- Has very small "pinpoint" pupils
- Has a seizure
- Has a high temperature, severe agitation, muscle stiffness or jerking, and heavy sweating (possible serotonin syndrome)

**If you have naloxone (Narcan), use it.** Naloxone is a nasal spray that reverses opioid effects, and it's been available over the counter in the US since 2023. Because part of tramadol's action isn't opioid-based, naloxone may only partly reverse it, and it does nothing for the alcohol. Use it anyway, call 911, and stay with the person. Keep them on their side, and be ready to give a second dose if they stop responding again, because naloxone can wear off before the drugs do.

If someone in your home takes tramadol or any other opioid, it's worth keeping naloxone around. Many pharmacies sell it without a prescription.

## Planning Around Events While You're on Tramadol

Most tramadol prescriptions are short, often a few days to a couple of weeks. The plan is to skip alcohol until your prescriber says it's safe to drink again.

- **Tell your prescriber about events ahead of time.** If something is coming up during your course, they can help you plan your pain treatment around it.
- **Choose alcohol-free drinks.** Non-alcoholic beer, wine, and spirits have gotten much better, and nobody at a party needs to know what's in your glass.
- **Ask whether you still need it.** If your pain has eased, ask your doctor whether you can switch to a different option. Don't stop a long course suddenly without asking, though.

For a broader look at common medicines and drinking, see our guide to [alcohol and medications](/never-hungover/alcohol-and-medications).

## Where DHM Fits (and Where It Doesn't)

We write a lot about DHM (dihydromyricetin), a plant compound studied for its effects on alcohol metabolism and hangovers. To be completely clear: **DHM has no role in making tramadol and alcohol safer.** There is no good evidence that it reduces opioid sedation, protects your breathing, lowers seizure risk, or prevents serotonin syndrome. Don't take it as a workaround to drink on tramadol.

Our [DHM medication interactions and safety guide](/never-hungover/dhm-medication-interactions-safety-guide-2025) covers what's known about DHM alongside prescription drugs, and the honest answer for many of them is that it hasn't been studied. If you're on tramadol, ask your pharmacist before adding any supplement.

Most of the evidence on DHM comes from animal and lab studies, with limited human data. Our [hangover prevention guide](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) covers the habits with the best evidence, for whenever your prescriber says drinking is safe again.

## The Bottom Line

- Tramadol is an opioid that also raises serotonin and can cause seizures. Alcohol adds to the sedation and breathing risk, and can make seizure and serotonin problems harder to spot.
- The FDA's boxed warning tells patients to avoid alcohol and other sedatives with tramadol. There's no amount that's known to be safe for everyone.
- Don't drink while you're on tramadol. Ask your prescriber or pharmacist when it's safe to drink again after your last dose.
- Never take tramadol for a hangover, and never take an extra dose after drinking.
- If someone is hard to wake, breathing slowly, or has a seizure after mixing the two, call 911 and use naloxone if you have it.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Can you drink alcohol while taking tramadol?**

No. The FDA's boxed warning for tramadol says that using it with alcohol or other central nervous system depressants can cause profound sedation, slowed breathing, coma, and death, and the label tells patients not to drink. Tramadol also raises seizure risk and can contribute to serotonin syndrome. Don't drink during your course, and ask your prescriber when it's safe to drink again after you stop.

**Is one drink on tramadol dangerous?**

Yes, it can be. There's no amount that's known to be safe. Your genes, your dose, how recently you took it, your age, and any other sedating medicines you take all change the risk. The official advice is to avoid alcohol entirely while on tramadol. If you've already had one drink, skip any more, don't drive, and ask a pharmacist before your next dose.

**How long after taking tramadol can I drink alcohol?**

There's no official waiting period, and it's not something to work out yourself. How long tramadol stays active depends on your dose, the form you take, your genes, your age, and your kidney and liver function. Ask your prescriber or pharmacist when it's safe to drink again after your last dose.

**How long after drinking can I take tramadol?**

Don't take tramadol while alcohol may still be in your system, and after a heavy night alcohol can still be present the next morning. If you're due a dose and you've been drinking, call your pharmacist before taking it.

**Can I take tramadol for a hangover?**

No. The morning after drinking, alcohol may still be in your blood, your seizure threshold may be lower from poor sleep and dehydration, and both tramadol and alcohol can lower blood sugar and cause nausea. Tramadol is also a controlled substance that should only be used as prescribed. For a hangover headache, try water, food, rest, and a single label dose of an over-the-counter pain reliever once the alcohol has cleared.

**What are the signs of a tramadol and alcohol overdose?**

Warning signs include extreme sleepiness or being unable to wake, slow or shallow breathing, gurgling or deep snoring sounds, blue or gray lips, pinpoint pupils, cold clammy skin, and seizures. Signs of serotonin syndrome include agitation, high fever, heavy sweating, a racing heart, and muscle stiffness or twitching. Call 911 right away, use naloxone (Narcan) if you have it, keep the person on their side, and stay with them.

**Does tramadol with alcohol cause seizures?**

Tramadol can cause seizures on its own, even at prescribed doses, and the risk rises with higher doses. Tramadol lowers the seizure threshold, and alcohol withdrawal, which begins as alcohol wears off, lowers it too. Its prescribing information lists alcohol and drug withdrawal among the situations that raise seizure risk further, so the two effects stack. If you've ever had a seizure or drink heavily most days, tell your doctor before starting tramadol.

**Can DHM make it safe to drink on tramadol?**

No. There is no good evidence that DHM reduces opioid sedation, protects breathing, lowers seizure risk, or prevents serotonin syndrome. Don't use any supplement as a reason to drink while taking tramadol, and ask your pharmacist before adding supplements to any prescription medicine.
